subject: Communication
title: The Anchoring Effect
description: Learn The Anchoring Effect in one minute.

hook.text: A car dealer shows you a $60,000 car first. Suddenly the $35,000 car feels like a steal.

buildup.text: Anchoring means the first number you hear becomes your mental reference point for everything after.

discovery.text: Kahneman and Tversky found that even random numbers — like a roulette wheel — bias later estimates.

twist.text: The anchor works even when people know it's arbitrary. Awareness doesn't immunize you from the effect.

climax.text: Retail 'was $100, now $40' uses anchoring. The original price exists only to make the sale price shine.

punchline.text: The first number wins — even when it's meaningless.

quiz.question: What does anchoring bias cause?
options: We rely too heavily on the first number we hear
We always choose the middle option

details.summary: The first number you hear in a negotiation sets an anchor that pulls all subsequent estimates toward it, even when the anchor is arbitrary. Real estate agents, salary negotiations, and retail pricing all exploit anchoring to shape what feels like a fair deal.
details.whyItMatters: Anchoring is one of the most robust cognitive biases. Whether you set the anchor or react to one determines your negotiation power.
takeaways: The first number mentioned becomes the reference point
Even random anchors influence estimates significantly
Setting the anchor first gives a strategic advantage

faq.question: How strong is the anchoring effect in studies?
faq.answer: Extremely strong. In one study, spinning a random number wheel before asking participants to estimate African nations in the UN shifted answers by over 20 percentage points. Even experts in their own fields fall prey to anchoring when given irrelevant numbers.

faq.question: How do you counter an unfavorable anchor?
faq.answer: Explicitly reject the anchor and reanchor with your own number supported by objective criteria. Avoid negotiating incrementally from their starting point. Research independent benchmarks beforehand so you have alternative reference points ready.
